name: Adam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so you can separate the line you give at work from what you think privately. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Adam, 27, and I lead the team keeping our company’s booking software running. I have a master’s degree and I’m good at tracing failures through old code, but the pay is low for a lead. I start by reading overnight error logs, then review fixes and talk with the support desk before customers wake up. I dislike surprise changes to the system and I have never used an AI coding tool. My savings would not cover one month of bills.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when a booking failure is fixed and nobody has to call the customer twice. I rent a small place alone near the bus stop, and there are few software jobs nearby. I send some money to my mother when her heating bill rises, though I cannot promise a fixed amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau sounds like the usual sales pitch cooling off. We would still need people who know the old booking system when a customer gets stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be glad if the work stayed familiar, but I would not call my own life secure. The company already delayed a pay review, and a broken laptop would empty my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking the overnight logs myself and keep my current job. On the next payday I’d set aside 25 for a laptop repair fund if the heating bill allows it. During the first year I’d ask my manager again for the overdue pay review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about money, though the AI part barely moves the needle. Familiar work does not make a thin account less thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the laptop fund when your mother needs help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my mother’s heating bill is high, the 25 stays with her. I would not pretend a savings plan is automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise the overdue pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show my manager the customer outages I prevented and ask for a date on the pay review. I would not threaten to leave when there are so few openings nearby.

say: I think **AI Plateau** leaves the old booking system needing experienced people.
I’d tell colleagues the **sales pitch** has run ahead of what the tool can do.
think: My **delayed pay review** and repair costs already threaten my small cushion.
I welcome familiar work, but my **income** does not feel secure.
do: **Keep** checking overnight booking logs and fixing faults myself.
**Set aside** 25 after payday for laptop repairs when family bills allow.
**Ask** for a date on the overdue pay review.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, even with little change from AI.
S0.quote: Familiar work does not make a thin account less thin.
fieldNote: The **baseline money worry** remains under AI Plateau: delayed pay and family heating bills eat his cushion.
He protects his **familiar workflow** and will ask for a review without threatening to quit.

steps.text: Keep checking overnight booking logs and repairing failures himself
Put 25 toward laptop repairs when family bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption is likely to make our bosses expect faster fixes. Software may write code and answer customers, but someone will still have to take responsibility when a booking goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my refusal to use the new tools could cost me the lead role. The company could stop replacing developers and put an AI answer in front of our support desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager which duties are changing before I sign up for training. If the team begins using an assistant, I’d sit beside Priya, our support lead, while she tests it on old customer cases. In the first year I’d learn only the approved tool well enough to review its answers, and cut my weekly takeaway meal to build a small buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious if the headcount starts shrinking, because there is nowhere nearby I can easily move. Waiting to test the new coding assistant could cost me my lead role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would carry the mistake when an AI answer is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya (our support lead) would have to explain a wrong AI answer to the customer, even if the company wrote the rule. I’d want her at the meeting where the new targets are set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first use of an AI tool look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d try the approved assistant on a copied test case, not on live customer data. If it gets the booking rule wrong, I’d save the example and show my manager.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to raise speed targets for code and customer replies.
I think someone still needs to take **responsibility** for failed bookings.
think: My **resistance** to new tools could put the lead role at risk.
I would face **few local alternatives** if developers shrink and support becomes automated.
do: **Ask** management which booking duties and staffing plans are changing.
**Test** the approved assistant with copied cases beside the support lead.
**Cut** one weekly takeaway meal during the first year to build a buffer.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts and conscious that delay may hurt me.
S1.quote: Waiting to test the new coding assistant could cost me my lead role.
fieldNote: His **public concern** is accountability, while privately he fears his refusal to use AI may cost his lead job.
He accepts a **narrow trial** only after seeing work changes and protecting customer data.

steps.text: Test the approved coding assistant on copied booking cases
Skip one weekly takeaway meal during the first year to build a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AGI by 2028 would make our software skills cheap very quickly. Thinking work in booking code changes by 2028; robots arriving around 2031 do not buy desk workers extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fear the company could keep one caretaker for the old system and dismiss the rest. I have maintained the old booking system for years, but I do not trust my lead title to protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d first ask for a written account of the company’s staffing plans and any severance terms. I’d stop optional spending and keep cash for rent; I cannot fund a new degree. In the first year after 2028, if the job goes, I’d apply for local technical support work and ask my mother whether I could stay with her temporarily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and probably lose sleep. Two years is too short to build a cushion from this wage, but I could still make calls and applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel my streaming subscriptions and put the saved money toward rent. I’d keep the bus pass because I need it for any job interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How real is staying with your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother has a spare room, but I would ask before treating it as an escape plan. She has heating costs of her own, and I would contribute when I could.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach booking code before hands-on robots arrive.
I’d ask for **written staffing** and severance terms.
think: I fear the firm may keep one **old-system caretaker** and let the rest go.
My lead role offers **no guarantee** of being kept.
do: **Request** written staffing and severance plans now.
**Cancel** streaming subscriptions to protect rent money.
**Apply** for technical support work and ask my mother about a temporary room if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely job loss and only two years to save.
S2.quote: I have maintained the old booking system for years, but I do not trust my lead title to protect me.
fieldNote: He correctly places the **desk-work shock** in 2028, with robots following around 2031.
His **family fallback** is conditional on his mother’s consent and finances; he would seek support work if dismissed.

steps.text: Cancel streaming subscriptions and hold the money for rent
Apply for local technical support roles if dismissed after 2028
Ask his mother about a temporary room if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives managers time to tell us the truth about staffing. The thinking part of our job changes by 2031; robots around 2034 are almost beside the point for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me find a steadier kind of technical work, but I dislike making a career bet on a forecast. I might waste three years hoping the booking system stays awkward enough to need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take one evening a month to learn the company’s server and network setup from our operations technician. I’d ask my manager for a paid course in system recovery; if refused, I’d use free material and keep notes on faults I resolved. In the first year after 2031, if code work is cut, I’d apply for operations support roles that still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, with more control than in the 2028 picture. Five years gives me time to test a path without leaving my wages now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you that retraining is worth the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to see a real operations vacancy and a written pay range before committing to a certificate. I will not spend rent money on a course advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move nearer family during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my mother before moving nearer her, because she may prefer her own space. For now I would keep the same flat and bus route.

say: I think **AGI by 2031** gives managers time to disclose a real staffing plan.
I see the **2034 robots** as little extra time for code workers.
think: I might cling to the **old booking system** too long.
I need an **actual vacancy** and pay range before spending on training for a new role.
do: **Learn** server recovery from the operations technician one evening monthly.
**Request** a paid recovery course, using free material if refused.
**Apply** for existing operations support jobs if code work shrinks after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, though five years gives room for a cautious trial.
S3.quote: I might waste three years hoping the booking system stays awkward enough to need me.
fieldNote: He can picture **gradual training** when the timeline offers five years and wages continue.
His **course choice** depends on employer funding or a real vacancy with a stated pay range.

steps.text: Study server recovery with the operations technician monthly
Apply for existing operations support roles if coding work shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 is far enough away to plan without wrecking this month’s work. Thinking AI reaches software by 2036 and robots around 2039 would matter more to other trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade helps, but I cannot assume this employer will still be here, or that I will have a pension waiting at 37. The postponed pay review still matters more this week than a distant date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the booking system and ask for the pay review in writing this quarter. If I get a raise, I’d save part of it toward three months of rent; if not, I’d check openings in the next city before deciding to move. In the first year after 2036, I’d choose among actual support or operations jobs rather than quit early on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about rent and long-run work, though a raise would help me steady things. AGI by 2036 still leaves my rent exposed to this year’s delayed pay review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a move to the next city realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If another city offers a job with enough pay to cover the higher rent, I’d consider moving. I would not move first and hope a job appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your mother’s heating bill fit the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A raise would mean I can help my mother with heating and still save something. Without one, I would keep helping when I can, but the emergency fund would grow slowly.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to plan alongside today’s booking work.
I’d keep asking for a **fair pay review** now.
think: I cannot assume my employer survives a decade or that a **pension** appears.
My **postponed raise** matters to rent and family support this week.
do: **Maintain** the booking system and request a written pay review this quarter.
**Save** part of any raise toward three months of rent.
**Check** next-city jobs before moving, only if pay covers higher rent.
feel: **Anxious** about rent and long-term work, with some control if pay improves.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 still leaves my rent exposed to this year’s delayed pay review.
fieldNote: The **ten-year horizon** lowers urgency but does not erase his immediate wage and family obligations.
He sets **conditions** for saving and moving: a raise, a real vacancy and enough pay for higher rent.

steps.text: Maintain the booking software and request a written pay review
Save part of any raise toward three months of rent
Check next-city software jobs before considering a move

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because software work would change before I could build much rent money. A written staffing decision, severance terms, and a paid course with a real job at the end would help. I cannot pay tuition out of an account that might not cover next month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to customers when the familiar old system fails. A cheap answer on a screen can still leave a person without a booking, and somebody has to answer the phone.

headlineQuote: A cheap answer on a screen can still leave a person without a booking, and somebody has to answer the phone.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and deep knowledge of a booking system’s older code.
His **low pay**, less than one month saved and occasional support for his mother make even AI Plateau financially anxious.
He has **never used AI** tools and fears that cautious habits could cost his lead role under Steady Disruption.
He would **test tools carefully**, learn operations work if funded or free, and seek another job only against real openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove software work before he has enough cash for rent.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms**, severance and a paid course linked to a real job would help.
